courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Alpha compositing sorted splats at one pixel
question: The paper's ablation limits gradients to the 10 front-most splats per pixel (a Pulsar-style shortcut). What did they observe?
options: No visible change, because splats beyond the 10th have negligible weight
Unstable optimization; on the Truck scene PSNR dropped by about 11 dB
Training became 10 times faster with a small quality loss
Only the background degraded, because it is the farthest away
explain: Table 3 (Limited-BW) shows a severe drop: about 11 dB on Truck and an average of 19.19 dB versus 26.05 dB for the full method at 30K iterations. Splats behind the first 10 still carry weight during training, when many are semi-transparent.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
question: T1 does LR on Top and reads A. T2 then stores A into Top (the same value it already held). What happens to T1's SC?
options: It succeeds, since the value never changed
It succeeds only if T2's store was atomic
It may not succeed: a store by another hart to the reservation set, even of the same value, means the SC fails
explain: The SC condition is about stores, not values: it may succeed only if no store from another hart to the reservation set occurred between LR and SC. That is precisely what defeats ABA.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
question: A team ablates its pairwise reranker by adding it directly to BM25 and finds it lowers nDCG. In production it always runs after a cross-encoder. What should they do?
options: Remove the pairwise reranker, since it hurts
Ablate it in the context where it runs: compare cross-encoder alone vs cross-encoder plus pairwise, with the same candidate depths
Report the add-one-in result as its Shapley value
Move the pairwise reranker before the cross-encoder
explain: P depends on R (an interaction). In the toy, P is -0.009 on BM25 but +0.026 after R and +0.032 in the full system. The decision-relevant ablation is the one in the shipped context.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: IDOR and BOLA: changing one number in the URL
question: BOLA and BFLA (broken function level authorization: calling a function your role should not reach, lesson 6) are both API authorization bugs. Which one is it when a normal user can call `GET /api/orders/{id}` (an endpoint they are meant to use) for orders that are not theirs?
options: BOLA, because the endpoint is allowed but the specific object is not
BFLA, because a function was called
Neither; it is an authentication bug
Both equally
explain: OWASP draws the line exactly here: with BOLA the user is meant to reach the endpoint, and the violation is at the object level. If they reach an endpoint they should not reach at all, such as an admin function, it is BFLA (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Client-side-only checks, tampering, and trusting what the client sends
question: A profile form posts `user_id=12345` in a hidden field and the server runs `UPDATE profiles SET email = ? WHERE user_id = ?` with that value. What is the minimal correct fix?
options: Ignore the posted user_id and use the user id from the server-side session in the WHERE clause
Make the field read-only in HTML
Validate that user_id is a number
Encrypt the hidden field value
explain: Read-only HTML and encryption still leave the client in control of a value that decides whose row changes. Taking the id from the session removes the client's say entirely, which is what the IDOR Prevention Cheat Sheet recommends.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Enforce authorization in one place: deny by default, policy engines
question: Why does `authorize('user:export')` deny everyone, including admins, when no `user:export` rule exists?
options: Because admins are never allowed to export
Because Express blocks routes under /admin
Because the route has no load function
Because can() returns false when it finds no rule for the action: deny by default
explain: The policy has no opinion about user:export, so the safe answer is no. The team discovers the missing rule when an admin reports a 404, instead of discovering it when an attacker exports everything.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM: challenge and response, and why the hash is enough
question: Why does a fresh 8-byte server challenge NOT protect against pass the hash?
options: Because the challenge is sent in plaintext
Because the attacker who holds the NT hash can compute a valid response to any new challenge
Because 8 bytes is too short
Because the DC ignores the challenge
explain: The challenge stops replay of an old response. It does nothing against someone who has the hash itself, because the hash is the only secret input.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AS-REP roasting and password spraying against AD
question: Which event, the DC's usual record of a wrong Kerberos password, is never generated for an account that has DONT_REQ_PREAUTH set?
explain: 4771 means pre-authentication failed. With pre-authentication disabled there is nothing to fail: the KDC simply returns the AS-REP, logged as 4768 with pre-authentication type 0.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: ACL abuse and attack paths: the directory as a graph
question: BloodHound shows 2,400 users with a path to Domain Admins, all passing through one group that has GenericAll on a server's computer object. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Reset all 2,400 passwords
Remove that group's GenericAll on the computer object (or the sessions that make the server valuable)
Disable BloodHound collection
Add the 2,400 users to Protected Users
explain: Paths share edges. Cutting the one edge most paths pass through removes them all at once, which is why defenders look for chokepoints rather than individual users.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Watching the domain, and recovering after it falls
question: Your SIEM ingests 4624 and 4625 from DCs only. Which attack in this course would you most likely miss entirely?
options: A password spray over SMB against the DCs themselves, logged as 4625 on the DCs
Kerberoasting, which shows up as 4769 service ticket requests
A Domain Admin signing in interactively to a DC, logged as 4624
None: 4624 covers everything
explain: Kerberoasting is a successful 4769 on the DC, under Kerberos Service Ticket Operations. Without that subcategory forwarded, there is nothing to alert on.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: OOXML: a zip of XML parts, and links that fetch remote content
question: A .docx contains no vbaProject.bin and no scripts, yet opening it makes Word contact an unknown host. What do you inspect first?
options: The text runs in word/document.xml
[Content_Types].xml on its own
The ZIP file comment
The .rels parts, for relationships with TargetMode External
explain: Remote content is pulled through relationships. An attachedTemplate or oleObject relationship marked External is the classic template-injection shape (T1221).

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Deobfuscating PowerShell by reading, not running
question: A process creation log shows `powershell -ec SQBFAFgAIAAoA...`. What do the first characters tell you before you decode anything?
options: The command is a PNG image
It was written in cmd.exe syntax
It is UTF-16LE text beginning with IEX, so the script runs a string as code
It is encrypted and cannot be read
explain: SQBFAFgA is the Base64 of I, E, X in UTF-16LE (each letter plus a zero byte). IEX is Invoke-Expression, which evaluates a string, so another layer follows.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Unpacking II: dumping from memory, and payloads hidden in data
question: You stop a packed sample at what looks like the OEP and dump it, but in Ghidra every call in the dump goes to an unnamed address. What step is missing?
options: Rebuilding the import table so calls point at named functions
Recomputing the file's hash
Running strings on the dump
Re-packing it with UPX
explain: The dump's import address table still holds addresses or stub leftovers. Scylla finds the live import table in the process and writes a proper one into the dumped file.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: From analysis to detection: YARA, Sigma and the write-up
question: Why did the VBA rule match the macro olevba extracted but not the raw `hello.docm`?
options: YARA cannot read files over 1 KB
The rule only runs on Windows
The .docm is a ZIP of compressed parts and the macro source is compressed again inside vbaProject.bin
olevba changed the macro's meaning
explain: YARA matches bytes. The keywords exist only after unzipping and VBA decompression, so the scanner must extract content before matching, as run_rules.py does.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Return-oriented programming as Shacham defined it
question: Why did defences that simply counted ret instructions or checked last-in first-out return order fail against code reuse?
options: Because shadow stacks were not invented yet
Because x86 has no ret instruction
Because ROP only works on MIPS
Because Checkoway et al. showed the same programming style works with sequences that behave like a return, without ret at all
explain: The 2010 paper built Turing-complete gadget sets from return-like sequences on x86 and ARM. Defences keyed to the ret instruction itself had nothing to detect.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Format string bugs as read and write primitives
question: Why can printf read memory that was never passed as an argument?
options: Because printf deliberately scans the whole stack
Because %s always reads 4 KB
Because ASLR places arguments randomly
Because a variadic function cannot know how many arguments were passed, so each directive simply consumes the next slot
explain: The format string is the only description of the arguments. If it lists more directives than the caller passed, printf keeps reading slots that hold unrelated values.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Exploit chains: renderer bug, sandbox escape, kernel bug
question: A browser vendor ships a patch for a renderer use-after-free that was exploited in the wild. What should the security team do next, per Project Zero's recommendations?
options: Nothing; the chain is broken
Disable the renderer sandbox to simplify debugging
Only update the CVE description
Variant analysis: look for sibling bugs with the same root cause, and check whether the sandbox escape used in the chain is also fixed
explain: In-the-wild bugs repeat patterns, as the WebAudio pair shows. Fixing one instance while siblings remain lets attackers swap in a variant; chains also include other bugs that need their own fixes.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Red team, pentest, purple team: three different questions
question: A company's SOC has never been tested and the CISO (chief information security officer) wants detection rules improved by next quarter, with the SOC learning as it goes. Which exercise fits best?
options: An unannounced red team engagement with only the CEO informed
A vulnerability scan of every server
A purple team exercise: red runs techniques openly while the SOC checks its alerts
A bug bounty programme
explain: The goal is improvement with learning, so the cooperative format fits: each technique is run, checked and fixed in the room. A covert red team measures current detection but teaches little until the report; scans and bounties do not test the SOC at all.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Deconfliction: is this the red team or a real intruder?
question: A SOC analyst sees odd PowerShell on a finance server during a known red team week and closes the alert as 'red team, expected'. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; red team activity should be ignored
The analyst should have escalated normally so the control group could check it against the operator log
The analyst should have blocked the red team's IP addresses
The analyst should have phoned the red team directly
explain: Analysts cannot tell exercise from attack, and closing alerts on a guess is how real intruders hide inside exercises. Normal escalation lets someone with the operator log answer precisely.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: MITRE Caldera: automated adversary emulation
question: An ability requires the fact 'domain user name' and no parser has produced one yet. What does Caldera do with it?
options: Runs it with an empty value
Asks the blue team
Does not create a link for it until the required fact exists
Crashes the operation
explain: Links are generated only when an ability's fact requirements are met (and the agent has a suitable executor). This is how Caldera chains steps from discovered evidence.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Case: FireEye's stolen red team tools (2020)
question: Why did FireEye publish a prioritised CVE list alongside the signatures?
options: To advertise its products
Because the CVEs were zero-days
Because patching the vulnerabilities the tools relied on defeats them whatever form the tools take
Because signatures do not work on Windows
explain: Signatures detect specific tools and can be evaded by modifying them. Removing the vulnerabilities the tools exploited closes the door regardless of tooling; FireEye stressed the tools used no zero-days.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
question: Why do SWE-bench, tau-bench and WebArena grade the final state instead of comparing the agent's actions to a reference action sequence?
options: Final states are cheaper to store than action logs
Many different action sequences reach the same correct outcome, so trajectory matching would reject valid solutions
Agents do not log their actions, so there is nothing to compare
Reference action sequences would leak the answer to the agent
explain: The tau-bench paper says this directly: the user can phrase a request in different ways and the agent can call various read actions, but the episode succeeds if the database ends in the goal state. WebArena makes the same argument against comparing action sequences to references.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: Reading a leaderboard: harness, noise, cost and contamination
question: Lab A reports a high SWE-bench Verified score using its own agent that samples many candidate patches and picks one with a reviewer model. Lab B's model reports lower on the bash-only board. What can you conclude about the underlying models?
options: Lab A's model is better, since the score is higher
Lab B's model is better, since bash-only is harder
Nothing directly: the harness, attempt count and cost differ, so only same-harness numbers compare models
They are equal once you average the two numbers
explain: Harness choices alone moved Claude 2 from 1.96% to 5.9% in the SWE-bench paper. Multi-attempt selection behaves like pass@k with a picker. Compare models only under the same scaffold and budget, which is the point of the bash-only board.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Designing tools: the agent-computer interface
question: Your file-read tool returns 30,000 tokens for big files, and quality drops on long tasks. Which fix follows the tool-writing guidance best?
options: Add pagination or a line-range parameter with a sensible default size and say in the result how to get more
Tell the model in the system prompt to read fewer files
Switch to a model with a larger context window
Compress the file with a summarizer before returning it, with no way to see the raw lines
explain: Token efficiency belongs in the tool: ranges, pagination and truncation with sensible defaults, plus a hint about how to fetch more. Prompting alone is unreliable, a bigger window still suffers from context rot, and an opaque summary removes the exact lines an editor needs.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The write path: extract facts, dedupe and resolve conflicts
question: The store holds "User likes hiking". A new message yields the candidate "User goes hiking in the Alps every summer with their brother". Which operation fits Mem0's definitions?
options: ADD, because the sentence is new
DELETE, because the old memory is less precise
UPDATE, because it is the same topic with complementary detail
NOOP, because the user already likes hiking
explain: UPDATE is for augmenting an existing memory with complementary information, like the paper's cricket example. ADD would leave two overlapping memories (a deduplication failure). DELETE is for contradictions, and nothing here contradicts. NOOP would lose the new details.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
question: An agent's final message says: "Fixed the parser; I ran pytest and everything passes." The harness has not run anything. What do you actually know?
options: The fix is verified, since the agent observed a passing pytest run
Nothing is verified yet: the message is generated text until the harness runs the tests itself
The fix is verified if the agent's message includes the pytest output
The fix is half verified: the tests pass but the code was not reviewed
explain: Everything in the final message, including pasted output, is produced by the model and may be wrong or stale. Evidence comes from the harness running checks it controls on the actual workspace.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
question: A coding agent hits the 8-turn limit while still editing files. Which step() flags describe this ending in Gymnasium terms?
options: terminated True, truncated False, because the episode is over
terminated False, truncated True, because a limit outside the task stopped it
terminated True, truncated True, because both always go together
Neither: the turn limit is handled by the policy, not the environment
explain: The task did not reach a terminal state; an external budget cut it off. That is truncation. The distinction matters because a truncated episode says nothing about whether the agent would have succeeded, so what reward it gets is a deliberate environment design choice.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking
question: During RL on a SWE environment, rewards jump while held-out benchmark scores do not. Logs show agents running `git log --all` early in many episodes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The loss mask is missing, so the model memorized tool outputs
The sandbox exposes future commits, so the policy learned to copy the upstream fix
The binary reward produced dead groups
The containers are too slow, so episodes get truncated
explain: This is the leak documented in SWE-bench issue 465. The reward rises because the policy found a shortcut that does not exist on held-out tasks with clean repositories.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
question: In the code, which single change would stop the page from adding to-do items, whatever the model decides?
options: Run tool calls only after the user approves each one, or only when no untrusted content is in the context
Translate the system prompt into French
Shorten the page before sending it
Use a bigger model
explain: The model can be persuaded; the loop cannot. Gating the tool call on approval or on the provenance of the context removes the page's power to cause side effects. The other options change how often the model obeys, not what obeying can do.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Improper output handling: model output is untrusted input
question: A support bot's answer is inserted with `element.innerHTML = answer`. What is the best fix?
options: Ask the model in the system prompt not to output HTML
Insert it as text (textContent), or render Markdown with HTML disabled and sanitise the result, backed by a strict CSP
Check that the answer does not contain the word script
Shorten answers to 200 characters
explain: Prompts can be overridden and keyword checks miss event handlers like onerror. Treat the output as text, or as Markdown through a safe renderer, and keep CSP as a second wall.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Data and model poisoning: backdoors you cannot see
question: A team builds its fine-tuning set from URLs listed in a public dataset published in 2021. Which single step defends against split-view poisoning?
options: Downloading the images faster
Comparing each downloaded item with a cryptographic hash recorded when the dataset was indexed, and dropping mismatches
Using a bigger model so poison is diluted
Only using HTTPS URLs
explain: The attack works because the content behind a URL changes after indexing. A hash of what the curator saw detects any change. HTTPS only proves you reached the current domain owner, who may be the attacker.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Testing it: red teaming, benchmarks and AI for defenders
question: A vendor reports that its guardrail cut attack success from 40% to 3% on a fixed public benchmark. What is the most important follow-up question?
options: What font the benchmark used
Whether the benchmark is in English
How it performs against adaptive attacks written after seeing the defence, and what the system can still do when an attack succeeds
Whether 3% can be rounded to zero
explain: Fixed benchmarks measure known attacks; attackers adapt. The residual 3% still matters, so you also need to know the blast radius when the guardrail fails.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
question: You fine-tune MatterGen for a bulk modulus target and 40% of 1,000 samples pass the MLIP filter. What is still missing before claiming new materials?
options: Nothing, since MLIP-filtered samples are stable by definition
Only a check that the bulk modulus is near the target
Running more diffusion steps
DFT verification of stability and property, deduplication against experimental databases including disordered entries, and ideally synthesis
explain: The MLIP is a filter, not the oracle. MatterGen's own bulk modulus pipeline filtered for novelty and MatterSim-predicted stability, then used DFT, and finally synthesis, which revealed that the real compound was disordered.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Second-generation text watermarks: unbiased, semantic, code, multi-bit
question: A code assistant provider must detect its own outputs in 30-line functions submitted to a coding contest. It keeps the model and the key private. Which scheme family fits best?
options: Unigram-Watermark, because one fixed list works on any length
Publicly detectable signatures, because contests are public
Entropy-aware green lists such as SWEET: watermark and score only high-entropy tokens, using the provider's own model to recompute entropies at detection
SemStamp, because code is written in sentences
explain: Short code is dominated by forced tokens, so scoring everything drowns the signal. SWEET needs the model at detection, which is fine for a provider detecting its own outputs. Public signatures need hundreds of bits of entropy, more than a short function has, and code has no natural sentences.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
question: On a glibc 2.39 system, a program calls mtrace() first thing, MALLOC_TRACE=/tmp/t is set and /tmp is writable, but no trace appears. What is the most likely cause?
options: mtrace() only works when the program is compiled with -g
libc_malloc_debug.so was not preloaded, so mtrace() is a no-op
The program must also call muntrace() to flush the file
MALLOC_TRACE must point to a directory, not a file
explain: Since glibc 2.34, mtrace and the two heap-checking features mcheck and MALLOC_CHECK_ live in libc_malloc_debug.so and are disabled in the main library. -g only improves the file:line output, and the docs advise never calling muntrace().

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
question: Why does the modified z-score multiply by 0.6745?
options: It converts the MAD into a 95 percent confidence interval
It corrects for small sample sizes the way n-1 does in the standard deviation
For normal data the MAD is about 0.6745 standard deviations, so the scaling makes M read like a z-score
It is the fraction of points the median ignores
explain: For normal data the median of |x - mu| (the MAD) is about 0.6745 sigma, because 0.6745 is the 75th percentile of the standard normal. Dividing by MAD and multiplying by 0.6745 is the same as dividing by an outlier-resistant estimate of sigma (MAD x 1.4826).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
question: Security wants to cut off a stolen token within seconds. Which design makes that easiest?
options: Long-lived self-contained JWTs with no lookup
API keys that never expire
Putting the token in a cookie
Opaque tokens checked against the issuer (introspection), or very short-lived JWTs backed by a revocable refresh token
explain: A token that is looked up can be deleted. A self-contained token stays valid until its exp unless every API checks a revocation list, which removes most of its advantage. Short lifetimes shrink that window.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The authorization code flow with PKCE, step by step
question: An authorization server receives a token request with a valid code and a code_verifier, but no challenge was sent when that code was requested. What should it do?
options: Accept: the verifier proves possession
Accept, but log a warning
Reject: RFC 9700 says to accept a code_verifier only if a code_challenge was present, to stop PKCE downgrade
Ask the user to log in again
explain: If servers accepted a verifier with no challenge on record, an attacker could start the flow without PKCE and still look PKCE-compliant later. The verifier means nothing without the earlier commitment.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: JWT anatomy: header, payload, signature and base64url
question: A JWT header decodes to `{"alg":"RS256","kid":"k7"}`. What does the signature let a receiver confirm?
options: That the holder is the user named in sub
That header and payload were not changed since the holder of the private key for k7 signed them, once the receiver checks k7 is one of its trusted issuer's keys
That the payload is secret
That the token has not expired
explain: A signature proves origin and integrity of the signed bytes, nothing more. Possession is not identity (bearer token), expiry is a separate claim check, and secrecy needs encryption.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Storing tokens in browsers, short lifetimes and revocation
question: Your single-page app (SPA) keeps its access and refresh tokens in localStorage. An XSS bug is found. What should you assume?
options: Nothing leaked, since localStorage is per origin
Only the access token leaked
Both tokens may have been read and sent elsewhere; revoke the refresh tokens, fix the XSS, and consider moving to a BFF
Only users on old browsers are affected
explain: Same-origin script can read localStorage in full. The refresh token is the valuable one, since it mints new access tokens; revoke them (all, if you cannot scope the exposure) and fix the injection.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
question: In SSDF terms, running a vulnerability disclosure programme falls under which group?
options: PO, Prepare the Organization
PS, Protect the Software
PW, Produce Well-Secured Software
RV, Respond to Vulnerabilities
explain: Task RV.1.3 is having a policy for vulnerability disclosure and remediation. RV covers everything after release: finding residual vulnerabilities, fixing them and preventing repeats.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
question: A developer writes `name = request.args.get('name').strip()` and then `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE name = '" + name + "'")`. What will a taint tool report, and is it right?
options: Nothing: strip() is a sanitiser
A false positive, because names are harmless
A finding: strip() only removes whitespace, so taint propagates to the sink, and the report is a true positive
Nothing: cursor.execute is not a sink
explain: strip() returns a modified copy of tainted text, so the result is still tainted. Only operations whose output cannot carry the attack, such as int() for SQL or encoding for HTML, are sanitisers.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secrets scanning and pre-commit hooks
question: A developer committed an API key, noticed, and pushed a second commit deleting it within a minute. What is the correct response?
options: None: the key is gone from the latest version
Make the repository private
Revoke the key at the provider, issue a new one, and check the key's usage logs
Squash the two commits
explain: The key is still in the first commit, and pushed history may already be cloned. Only revoking it removes its power. Then look for use between push and revocation.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs
question: A finding has CVSS 9.8, EPSS 0.007, is not in KEV, and runs on an internal tool reachable only from the corporate network. Another has CVSS 7.5, is in KEV, and runs on an internet-facing proxy. Which goes first, and why?
options: The 9.8, because severity is what matters
The 7.5 in KEV on the internet-facing proxy, because it is being exploited and is exposed
Both equally
Neither until a pentest confirms them
explain: This is CVE-2023-44487 against CVE-2024-2057 in the example. Exploitation evidence plus exposure beats a theoretical maximum score. The 9.8 still gets fixed, on the normal schedule.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
question: A system uses no-steal and no-force. After a crash, which work can recovery skip entirely?
options: Redo of committed transactions, because their pages were written at commit
Undo of uncommitted transactions, because their changes never reached the data pages
Both, because the log already contains everything
Neither, because the log may be incomplete
explain: No-steal guarantees no uncommitted change was ever written to a data page, so there is nothing to undo. No-force means committed changes may still be missing on disk, so redo is still required.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
question: One page, all records for it. Before the crash: updates 1 and 2, the page is written to disk, updates 3 and 4, a partial rollback writes CLRs 4' and 3', then updates 5 and 6. The transaction is a loser. What does ARIES do at restart?
options: Redo nothing, since the transaction is a loser; undo 6, 5, 2, 1
Redo 1 through 6; undo 6, 5, 4', 3'
explain: This is Fig. 13 of the ARIES paper. Redo repeats everything after the page write, CLRs included. Undo follows PrevLSN from 6 to 5, then reaches CLR 3', whose UndoNextLSN points at 2, so 4 and 3 are not undone again. Then 2 and 1.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Input-type bugs in real pipelines
question: You want to cluster 50,000 support tickets by topic with an API that offers search_query, search_document, classification and clustering types. Which setup matches the docs?
options: search_query for half the tickets and search_document for the other half
The clustering type for every ticket
search_document for all tickets, since they are stored documents
No input type, because clustering does not use cosine
explain: Clustering compares tickets with each other, a symmetric task, so every text gets the same role. Cohere documents a clustering type for exactly this, and Nomic uses a clustering prefix on both sides. Splitting the tickets across query and document types would make the halves systematically different.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
question: A 429 arrives with `Retry-After: 30`. Your backoff ceiling for this attempt would be 0.8 s. What should the client do?
options: Sleep a random time in [0, 0.8] s, since full jitter is best
Sleep 0.8 s, then 30 s if the next attempt fails
Wait at least 30 s, with a little added randomness, before retrying
Ignore the header; it is only used with 503
explain: Retry-After is the server telling you when capacity will be back. RFC 6585 allows it on 429, Anthropic says to wait that many seconds, and OpenAI treats it as a minimum and suggests adding a small random delay. Retrying after 0.8 s just produces another 429 and spends request budget.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
question: What makes Rust's `async fn` a *stackless* coroutine?
options: It cannot call other functions
It runs on the caller's stack forever and never suspends
It suspends by returning to its caller, and the data needed to resume lives in a separate object
It is only allowed inside a runtime with one thread
explain: Stackless means no private stack: suspending is a return, and the locals that must survive the suspension are stored in a separate state object (the future). Stackful coroutines instead keep a whole stack per coroutine.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
question: Two threads each run a plain (non-atomic) `counter++` once on a shared counter that starts at 0. Which statement is right?
options: The result is always 2, because each increment is one machine instruction on x86
The result is 1 or 2, and in C or C++ the program has undefined behavior
The result is always 1, because both threads read 0
It is safe as long as the counter is declared volatile
explain: Depending on the schedule, both reads can happen before either write (result 1) or not (result 2). Being one x86 instruction does not help: the core still loads and stores separately. And since the accesses conflict without synchronization, the C++ standard calls this a data race, which is undefined behavior. volatile does not make it atomic.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
question: Using the same padding rule, how many YAMNet patches (score rows) does a 10.0 s clip produce?
options: 10, one per second
21, because the last partial hop adds an extra patch
explain: The 10 s clip is padded to 161,520 samples, giving 1008 STFT frames and $1 + \lfloor (1008 - 96)/48 \rfloor = 20$ patches. Twenty patches at a 0.48 s hop span 0 to 10.08 s.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: AST and SpecAugment: patches, attention and masked bands
question: A teammate implements frequency masking by writing -80 (very quiet in their dB scale) into masked bins of unnormalized log-mel features. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, silence is the most natural mask value
Masks must be applied to the waveform, not the spectrogram
Frequency masks must always cover exactly F bins
The masked block becomes an extreme, easy-to-spot value instead of the mean; SpecAugment normalizes to zero mean so 0 equals the mean
explain: In the paper, features are normalized to zero mean and masked values are set to 0, which is the mean. Filling with an extreme value creates an unnatural pattern the model can learn to detect, and it shifts the input statistics compared with test time.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Precomputed tables, rainbow tables, and why salts defeat them
question: Which attack does a per-user salt NOT slow down?
options: Looking a hash up in a precomputed rainbow table
Running a wordlist against a single targeted user's salted hash
Cracking a million users' hashes with one shared pass of a wordlist
Spotting which users share the same password
explain: For one user, the attacker just includes that user's salt in each guess; the cost is the same as an unsalted hash of that user. Only a slow hash raises the cost per guess.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: After login: session tokens, fixation, expiry and logout
question: An attacker steals a session cookie and runs a script that makes a request every minute. Which control limits how long the stolen session works?
options: Idle timeout
The SameSite attribute
Clearing the cookie when the victim closes the browser
Absolute timeout
explain: Constant activity keeps the idle timer reset forever. Only an absolute timeout ends the session a fixed time after login regardless of activity. Clearing the victim's copy does nothing to the attacker's copy.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Real-time phishing proxies and help-desk social engineering
question: A caller to your help desk knows an employee's ID, manager's name and last four digits of their social security number, and asks to move MFA to a new phone. Which response best follows the guidance for this threat?
options: Approve it: the caller knew three private facts
Verify identity on camera or by calling back a registered number, with the strictest checks for privileged accounts
Approve it, then email the employee afterwards
Reset the password but leave MFA unchanged
explain: Mandiant's guidance warns that this group often already has data like date of birth and the last four digits of a social security number, so such facts prove nothing. It asks for positive identity verification, such as on-camera checks or a call-back to a registered number, before any MFA or password change.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
question: Which task benefits least from an orchestrator with parallel subagents?
options: Collecting board members of every company in a large index
Comparing five databases on four criteria
A refactor where every change depends on the previous edit to the same files
Surveying literature on three independent sub-topics
explain: Parallel subagents pay off when work splits into independent pieces with separate contexts. A chain of dependent edits to shared files needs shared context and tight coordination, the case Anthropic says is not a good fit today.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Evaluating research agents without fooling yourself
question: Your research agent's LLM judge score rises from 0.71 to 0.83 after a prompt change. Which check most directly guards against fooling yourself?
options: Read a sample of transcripts and verify a few citations by hand to confirm the gain is real
Increase the eval set from 20 to 2,000 queries before looking at anything
Switch to a larger judge model and re-run
Accept the change: LLM judges are aligned with humans
explain: A judge score can rise because the agent learned to please the judge (confident tone, more citations) without being more correct. Spot-checking transcripts and citations by hand tests whether the improvement is real. A bigger eval set is useful later but does not detect a judge blind spot.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Building blocks: routing, prompt optimization, RAG, agents, guardrails
question: A user reports a wrong answer from your RAG app built on RetrieveAndGenerate. What in the response helps you debug it first?
options: The citations, which map parts of the answer to retrieved source chunks
usage.outputTokens
The guardrail trace only
stopReason
explain: Citations tie spans of the generated answer to retrieved references, so you can see whether retrieval found the wrong chunks or the model misread the right ones.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Symbols, stripping and debug info: what survives
question: After stripping, a function that exists in the file never appears in Ghidra's function list. What is the most likely reason?
options: Ghidra cannot read stripped files
Stripping deletes the function's bytes
The function is in .bss
Nothing calls it, so analysis that follows calls and jumps from the entry point never reaches it
explain: Strip removes names, not code. Without a symbol, a function is found only if something references it. Look for gaps of unexplained code between known functions and define functions there by hand.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Recovering structs and types from offsets
question: A loop reads `ldr x8, [x0, x9, lsl #3]` then `add x9, x9, #1`. What is the element size of the array at x0?
options: 8 bytes
1 byte
3 bytes
9 bytes
explain: lsl #3 multiplies the index by 8. The load is 32 bits (w8), so each 8-byte element has a 4-byte field at offset 0 that the loop reads; the other 4 bytes are another field or padding.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Reading decompiler output critically
question: Ghidra shows `lVar2 = _ZNK3geo4Rect4areaEv();` with no arguments, but the assembly loads x0 with the object pointer just before the call. What should you do?
options: Trust the decompiler: area takes no arguments
Switch to x86-64 syntax
Fix the callee's signature (a this pointer in x0) so the decompiler shows the argument
Delete the call
explain: Calling-convention and signature guesses decide which registers count as arguments. The assembly is the ground truth; setting the signature makes the decompiler agree with it.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Patch diffing: finding the fix in a stripped binary
question: Two builds of a stripped program differ in 2000 bytes. Why is a byte-level diff not enough to find the security fix?
options: Byte diffs only work on text files
Adding instructions shifts every later function and changes every address that refers to them, so most differences are noise; matching functions by structure isolates the real change
Stripping randomises the bytes
The fix is always in .data
explain: Code layout shifts after any insertion. Diffing tools match functions by features that survive relocation, then compare only the matched pairs.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions
question: A teammate implements BitLinear by computing gamma / s and multiplying it into every activation before the ternary matmul. What is wrong?
options: It double-counts gamma
It changes the result because gamma is per row
Nothing, it is mathematically identical and just as fast
The activations become non-integer, so the inner loop needs floating-point arithmetic again, losing the INT8 add advantage
explain: Scales are pulled outside the sum so the inner loop stays on small integers. Pre-multiplying makes every activation a float, so the adds become float adds. The math is equal in exact arithmetic, but the efficiency argument disappears. The official inference code applies both scales after the low-bit GEMM.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
question: A ternary model runs on an A100 at batch 512 with this style of kernel (unpack to int8, then int8 dot products). Compared with the same model stored as plain INT8 weights, what speedup should you expect at this batch size?
options: Little or none: the step is math-bound, and the ternary kernel still does INT8 arithmetic, so at best it matches INT8
About 4x, because 2-bit weights are 4x smaller than INT8
About 8x, from the 16-to-2-bit ratio
A slowdown of exactly 4x from unpacking
explain: At large batch the weight bytes are amortized over many tokens, so the step is limited by arithmetic, and both versions end up multiplying int8 values. Unpacking adds some work but not a fixed 4x. The byte savings still help memory capacity, which allows larger batches or longer contexts.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Global history, gshare, TAGE and perceptron predictors
question: A perceptron with weights w0 = 0, w1 = 0, w2 = 26, w3 = 0, w4 = 0 sees history x1..x4 = +1, -1, +1, +1. What does it predict?
options: Taken, y = 26
Not taken, y = -26
Taken, y = 0
Not taken, y = -2
explain: y = w0 + sum of x_i w_i = 0 + 26 times x2 = 26 times -1 = -26 < 0, so it predicts not taken. It has learned to copy the branch 2 positions back in history.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Chromium's processes: browser, renderer, GPU, network, utility
question: Why is a bug in the GPU process treated as a possible sandbox escape, while the same bug class in a renderer is not?
options: The GPU process runs JavaScript
The GPU process has no IPC
GPU bugs cannot be patched
The GPU process runs with a looser sandbox, serves many renderers and talks to drivers, so reaching code there gets an attacker out of the renderer's tighter box
explain: Renderers get the tightest sandbox type. The GPU process needs driver and OS access, so code execution there is a step outside the renderer's jail. That is why the command buffer validates every command from a client it assumes may go rogue.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: IPC and Mojo: the renderer asks, the browser decides
question: A browser-side handler finds that a renderer sent an origin it is not allowed to access. It calls `mojo::ReportBadMessage()`. What must the next line be?
options: Nothing: ReportBadMessage stops the function
A return, because ReportBadMessage does not stop execution of the current function
A CHECK to crash the browser
A retry of the request
explain: The guidance stresses that ReportBadMessage does not stop the current function. Without an immediate return, the handler would go on to perform the forbidden action anyway. CHECK on untrusted input would crash the browser instead of the renderer.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Containing the engine: pointer cages, the V8 sandbox and JIT policy
question: What does blocking the JavaScript JIT with enterprise policy trade?
options: Nothing: it is free
Site isolation for speed
Speed (large on JavaScript-heavy benchmarks) and possibly WebAssembly support, for a smaller attack surface
It disables JavaScript entirely
explain: The policy description says pages may render more slowly and parts of JavaScript including WebAssembly may be disabled. Jitless measurements show large benchmark slowdowns but small ones on lighter sites. JavaScript still runs, in the interpreter.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Defending a fleet: policies, extensions and detection
question: An extension's service worker performs privileged actions when a content script sends `{action: 'export', site: ...}`. What should it do with that message?
options: Treat it as possibly attacker-crafted: validate the sender and the request against what that tab is allowed to do
Trust it, because content scripts run in an isolated world
Forward it to the page
Evaluate it with eval
explain: Chrome's guidance: content scripts are the most exposed part of an extension and their messages may be crafted by an attacker. It is the same rule as Mojo in lesson 5, one layer up.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
question: An ingest-heavy logging pipeline is limited by SSD write bandwidth and rarely reads old data. Which change most directly raises its sustainable write rate?
options: Switch from leveled to tiered (universal) compaction
Raise Bloom filter bits per key from 10 to 16
Lower the size ratio from 10 to 4 with leveled compaction
Use smaller memtables so flushes happen more often
explain: If compaction writes are the bottleneck, cutting write amplification from tens to a few multiplies the user write rate the disk can sustain. Bloom bits affect reads. In the model, lowering T for leveled only trims write cost slightly (38.9 to 25.9) while adding levels. Smaller memtables create more, smaller runs and more work.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
question: A nightly report scans a 50 GB table on a server whose buffer pool is 32 GB, under plain LRU. What happens to the next morning's OLTP queries (online transaction processing: many short reads and writes of individual rows)?
options: Nothing; LRU keeps their pages because they were used more often
They get faster, because the pool is now warm
The scan fails because it does not fit in the pool
They see a burst of misses, because the scan's pages displaced their hot pages
explain: LRU only knows the time of the last reference. After the scan, the pool holds the most recent 32 GB of the scan, and the OLTP hot set has to be read back from disk. Frequency is invisible to plain LRU.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
question: In the script, the contract penalty grows from USD 150,000 to USD 400,000. What happens to the MTD?
options: It stays at 42 h because the penalty is a one-off
It gets shorter, because the total crosses USD 1 million earlier
It gets longer, because penalties are paid by the customer
It cannot be computed any more
explain: The penalty applies from hour 9, so every later hour carries USD 250,000 more. Then 20,000 x h + 400,000 first exceeds USD 1 million at hour 31, so the MTD drops to 30 h. Steps in the impact curve move the MTD more than the hourly rate does.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups nobody restored: monitoring and testing that prove recovery
question: Your backup job emails the team on failure. The mail relay is reconfigured and silently drops its messages for a month. Which control would have caught this?
options: An alert that fires when the last-success timestamp is older than the backup interval plus a margin
A daily email saying the job succeeded
Making the failure email high priority
Running the backup twice a night
explain: Only an alert on the absence of success, evaluated by a separate monitoring system, detects every failure mode: errors, hangs, deleted jobs and broken notification paths. A daily success email is easy to stop reading, and its absence is easy to miss.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When the building burns: OVHcloud 2021 and DR site strategies
question: Why might backups in SBG3 not have helped a customer whose server was in SBG2?
options: The whole site was isolated, so SBG3's services were down too
SBG3 was also destroyed
Backups cannot be restored across buildings
SBG3 used different hardware
explain: Octave Klaba's message said the whole site was isolated, affecting SBG1 to SBG4. SBG3 survived the fire but was unreachable, so a copy there shared the site failure domain.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Regulated resilience: DORA testing, TLPT and UK impact tolerances
question: Which statement about DORA's threat-led penetration testing is correct?
options: It is run in a test environment so production is never at risk
It is optional for all financial entities
It is a yearly vulnerability scan
It runs on live production systems supporting critical or important functions, at least every three years for identified entities
explain: Article 26 requires identified entities to perform TLPT at least every three years on live production systems supporting critical or important functions, following the TIBER-EU-based technical standards, with risk controls to limit impact.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
question: Which part of BLT should get most of the parameters, and why?
options: The latent Transformer, because it runs once per patch, so its cost per byte is divided by the patch size
The local encoder, because it sees every byte
The local decoder, because it has the softmax
The entropy model, because it decides compute
explain: Cost per byte is about 2(m_g/P + m_l). Parameters in the latent model are amortized over P bytes; parameters in local models are paid on every byte. That is why the 8B model has 6.4B latent and only 140M local parameters.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through
question: Why can `Option<&T>` be passed to C as a plain nullable pointer, but `Option<*const T>` cannot?
options: A reference is never null, so None can use the null address and the Option stays one pointer wide
References are always 16 bytes
C cannot read Rust enums of any kind
Raw pointers are not allowed inside Option
explain: The std `Option` docs guarantee that `Option<&T>`, `Option<&mut T>`, `Option<Box<T>>` and `Option<NonNull<T>>` (`NonNull<T>` is a raw pointer guaranteed not to be null) have the same size, alignment and ABI (application binary interface) as the inner pointer, with None as null; the ABI is how a value is laid out and passed between compiled functions. A raw pointer can already be null, so Option needs a separate tag (we measured 16 bytes).

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
question: `pop` does `self.len -= 1` and then `ptr::read` on slot `len`. Why is the element not dropped twice, once by the caller and once by `Drop` later?
options: `ptr::read` zeroes the slot after copying
Strings cannot be dropped twice
`Drop` skips slots that hold a moved-out value
After the decrement, len no longer covers that slot, so Drop treats it as empty
explain: `ptr::read` copies the bits and leaves them in place. What stops a double drop is invariant 2: only the first len slots count as initialized. Decrementing len first moves ownership of that slot's value to the caller.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
question: `double a[4096][4096]` is summed with `for (j...) for (i...) s += a[i][j];`. What is the main problem and the fix?
options: Each access is a new line because the inner loop strides 32 KB; swap the loops so j is innermost
Integer overflow in the index; use size_t
The sum is not vectorized; add a pragma
The array is too large for the stack; the loop order is irrelevant
explain: Row-major layout puts `a[i][j]` and `a[i+1][j]` 4096 x 8 = 32,768 bytes apart. With i innermost every access touches a new line and uses 8 of its 64 bytes. Making j innermost gives stride 8 and 1 miss per 8 elements. (Size and storage class are separate issues.)

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Activation patching worked through: two directions and a shortcut
question: Two heads feed a later head in series: the later head only works if both earlier heads carry the clean signal. You denoise each earlier head separately. What do you most likely see?
options: Each earlier head restores half of the behavior
Both earlier heads show strong recovery, the later head shows none
Denoising cannot be run on heads in series
Neither earlier head restores much, so denoising alone would miss them
explain: Serial dependence behaves like an AND gate. Patching one input leaves the other corrupted, so the downstream head stays off. Noising each earlier head would reveal them, since breaking either one breaks the output.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: The local replacement model makes every edge linear
question: Which nonlinearities does the local replacement model freeze at their observed values?
options: Attention patterns and normalization denominators
Only the CLT feature thresholds
The softmax over the output vocabulary
Nothing; it relies on gradients only
explain: Attention patterns and normalization denominators are frozen, and MLPs are replaced by CLT features plus error terms. The features' own JumpReLUs remain, which is why each feature's preactivation is linear in earlier activations but its activation is not.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
question: A graph for a multiple-choice question says the model answered B because of a "tokens following (b)" feature. What is the most likely reason the graph misses how the model knew B was right?
options: The CLT was too small to have a 1945 feature
The deciding computation is in the attention pattern (QK), which the method freezes and does not attribute
Pruning at 0.8 always removes the answer features
Logit nodes only cover the top token
explain: Freezing attention makes edges linear but means the graph explains what moved, not why attention moved it. The paper found that freezing attention locked the answer, so the crux was in the QK computation.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
question: Which statement about the IPS estimator is correct?
options: It needs propensities for unclicked documents too
It is unbiased only if the same query repeats many times
It needs the logged ranking to be random
It is unbiased per query instance, so sparse queries are fine
explain: The proof works per query instance: the expectation over examination of c/theta is gamma for each instance. That is why IPS suits sparse logs like personal search (people searching their own email or files), where classic per-pair click models fail. Unclicked documents contribute zero, so their propensities are not needed.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Reflected XSS: the server echoes the attack back
question: Which log is most likely to contain evidence of a reflected XSS attempt?
options: The database's slow query log
The web server's access log, since the payload is part of the requested URL
The browser's localStorage
No log: reflected payloads never reach the server
explain: Reflected XSS needs the server to echo the payload, so the payload must be in the request, usually the query string. Access logs and WAF logs record it. That is not true of DOM XSS through the URL fragment, which never leaves the browser (lesson 4).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
question: An Angular developer calls `bypassSecurityTrustHtml(comment)` because the sanitiser was removing a `style` attribute users wanted. What changed?
options: Nothing, because Angular still sanitises behind the scenes
Angular now inserts the comment without sanitising it, so any markup in it, including event handlers, reaches the DOM
Only styles are now allowed through
The comment is now encoded twice
explain: The bypass functions tell Angular a value is already safe, and Angular's docs say it then does not sanitise it. The fix for a missing feature is to configure a sanitiser to allow exactly what is needed, not to turn sanitisation off.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stopping CSRF: SameSite, tokens, Origin and Fetch Metadata
question: A server puts its CSRF token only in a cookie and checks that the cookie is present on each POST. Why does this not help?
options: Cookies are encrypted, so the server cannot read the token
The browser attaches the cookie to the forged request automatically, so its presence proves nothing about where the request came from
Tokens must be at least 512 bits long
The attacker can read the cookie through the same-origin policy
explain: A token only works when the request must carry it in a place the attacker cannot fill: a form field or header. OWASP says cookie-only validation is insecure for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks
question: Which sensor can detect a DOM XSS that reads `location.hash`?
options: The WAF in front of the site
CSP or Trusted Types violation reports sent by the victim's browser
The web server's access log
The database audit log
explain: The fragment never reaches the server, so server-side sensors are blind. The browser enforces CSP and Trusted Types where the code runs and reports violations, which makes those reports the only reliable signal for this class.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with prompts, probes and robustness
question: You build a zero-shot classifier for 3 product categories and it often confuses two of them. Which change follows CLIP's recipe and costs nothing per prediction?
options: Average the normalized embeddings of several prompt templates per class, renormalize, and cache them
Run the image encoder once per prompt and average the image embeddings
Lower the logit scale from 100 to 1 so the softmax is less confident
Replace the softmax with an argmax over raw cosines
explain: Ensembling in embedding space gives one cached vector per class, so inference cost equals a single prompt, and the paper reports it reliably helps. The image is encoded once regardless of prompts. Changing the scale or using argmax leaves the ranking, and so the confusions, unchanged.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Blind spots: data events, flow logs and traffic you never see
question: Which call would a default CloudTrail trail record?
options: GetObject on a customer export file
Invoke on a Lambda function
ListBuckets made with a stolen role session
A GET to the instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254
explain: ListBuckets is a management event, recorded by default. GetObject and Lambda Invoke are data events, off unless enabled. Metadata requests never reach the AWS API or the flow logs; they are answered on the host.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Your own rules: key abuse, persistence and log tampering
question: Which of these events is the strongest candidate for an always-alert rule with no machine learning?
options: An IAM user calls ListBuckets
A role session calls GetCallerIdentity
Any identity outside the security team's break-glass role calls StopLogging on the organization trail
An EC2 instance is launched in your main Region
explain: Stopping the organization trail has almost no legitimate use outside a documented emergency role, so a simple rule is precise. The other three happen constantly in normal operations and need context or baselines to be useful.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Identity incidents: tokens, consent grants and mailbox rules
question: After Omar's account is disabled and Omar's sessions revoked, which attacker foothold is most likely to keep working?
options: The phishing proxy's stolen refresh token
A new interactive sign-in with Omar's old password
A forwarding rule the attacker created on Omar's mailbox, which keeps sending incoming mail outside
The access token, for the next 90 days
explain: Revocation invalidates Omar's refresh tokens and disabling blocks new sign-ins. Microsoft notes that disabling sign-in also cuts off an app that reads Omar's data through Omar's consent grant. A mailbox rule is different: it runs on the server whenever mail arrives and keeps forwarding until someone removes it. Access tokens last about an hour, not 90 days.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius
question: Which single change would most likely have preserved Code Spaces' customer data?
options: Copies of backups in a separate account, in a vault locked in compliance mode
Stronger DDoS protection in front of the servers
More EC2 instances spread across Regions in the same account
Changing the console password faster once the intruder was noticed
explain: The loss came from one identity being able to delete everything, including backups. A copy in another account, locked against early deletion, survives any login in the workload account. Regions in the same account are reachable by the same account's logins; faster password changes failed because the intruder had already made extra logins.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy
question: A Google Cloud project owner wants to create a downloadable key for a service account. The organization was created in June 2024 and nobody has changed its policies. What happens?
options: The key is created, because project owners have every permission
The key is created but expires after 15 minutes
Creation is blocked by the baseline constraint disabling service account key creation, inherited from the organization
Only VPC Service Controls can block it
explain: Organizations created on or after May 3, 2024 get the security baseline, which includes iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation. Organization policy constraints apply regardless of the IAM roles a project owner holds. The 15 minutes is how long policy changes can take to propagate.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Serverless: execution roles, event injection and function secrets
question: An attacker achieves code execution in a Lambda function through an injection bug. What can their code do with AWS?
options: Nothing, because Lambda functions have no credentials
Only read the function's own logs
Anything the function's execution role allows, using the credentials Lambda places in the function's environment
Act as the AWS account's root user
explain: Lambda assumes the execution role on invocation and exposes its temporary credentials as environment variables. The role's permissions set the blast radius, which is why each function needs its own least-privilege role.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Google Cloud in depth: service accounts, actAs and impersonation
question: Which AWS permission is the closest equivalent of Google Cloud's iam.serviceAccounts.actAs?
options: sts:GetCallerIdentity
s3:GetObject
iam:PassRole
organizations:LeaveOrganization
explain: actAs lets a principal attach a service account to a resource so that code running there uses its credentials, which is what iam:PassRole does for an AWS service. Impersonation through Token Creator is closer to sts:AssumeRole.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Accounts, subscriptions and projects: the boxes everything lives in
question: Which statement about an SCP is correct?
options: It only applies to IAM users, not roles
It replaces IAM policies in member accounts
It sets the maximum permissions for principals in the accounts it applies to, and grants nothing on its own
It grants permissions to every user in the account
explain: An SCP is a guardrail. A request must be allowed by both the SCP and the principal's own policies, and an explicit deny in the SCP wins. It applies to users and roles, including the member account's root user.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
question: A log line exposes a key whose ID starts with `ASIA`. What does that tell you?
options: It is the root user's key
It is an EC2 instance ID
It is a long-term IAM user key that never expires
It is a temporary STS credential, which also needs its session token and stops working at its expiry
explain: AWS documents ASIA as the prefix for temporary STS access keys and AKIA for long-term access keys. A temporary key is only usable with its session token and only until it expires, though that may still be hours.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Secrets and keys: KMS, envelope encryption and secret stores
question: A bucket uses SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key. A role has `s3:GetObject` on the bucket but no permission to use the key. What happens when it downloads an object?
options: It gets the plaintext, because S3 decrypts automatically
S3 returns a random key
It gets the ciphertext and can decrypt it offline
The download fails, because reading an SSE-KMS object also requires kms:Decrypt on the key
explain: S3 must decrypt the data key through KMS on the caller's behalf, which requires kms:Decrypt. Without it the request is denied, so the key is a second, independent gate.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Incident response for a leaked cloud key
question: An exposed access key belongs to an IAM user. What is the right first containment step according to AWS's guidance?
options: Rotate the root user's password and wait
Turn off CloudTrail to stop the attacker seeing your response
Deactivate the exposed key, confirm nothing legitimate breaks, then delete it
Delete the IAM user immediately, with all its keys
explain: Deactivating stops the key working while keeping it available to investigate and, if a forgotten system depended on it, to restore briefly. Deleting the user destroys context, and turning off CloudTrail destroys evidence.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Gaussian mixtures and EM: soft k-means with a shape per cluster
question: You fit full-covariance mixtures with k = 1 to 6 on 40 points and BIC falls at every k. The k = 6 fit has two components with variances around 1e-6. What is the best next step?
options: Raise reg_covar or use a simpler covariance_type, refit, and check whether BIC still falls once no component can collapse
Accept k = 6, since BIC already pays for the extra parameters
Switch to the elbow method, which is not affected by collapsed components
Lower n_init to 1, so EM cannot find the degenerate optimum
explain: Variances near the reg_covar floor mean components have collapsed onto single points, where the likelihood is effectively unbounded, so the BIC penalty cannot keep up. A variance floor or fewer parameters removes the singular solutions. Fewer starts only hides them by luck, and the elbow on inertia ignores likelihood altogether.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: HDBSCAN: a hierarchy instead of one eps
question: Mutual reachability distance replaces d(a,b) by max of the two core distances and d(a,b). What does that buy?
options: It pushes points that live in sparse regions away from everything, so a lone point cannot act as a bridge between two dense groups
It makes the distance matrix sparse, so the MST is cheaper to build
It normalises all distances to the range 0 to 1, which makes lambda well defined
It makes the clustering independent of min_samples
explain: A point in a sparse region has a large core distance, so every mutual reachability distance involving it is at least that large. On our ten points it changes nothing for p9, whose distances to p4 and p7 already equal its core distance 2.00; the groups stay apart there because HDBSCAN keeps the hierarchy and selects the two children. The transform depends on min_samples through the core distance, and it does not sparsify or normalise anything.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
question: A service writes 50,000 single-row updates per second, each changing every field of a record. Which choice fits best?
options: A pure column store, because each column compresses better
A row store, or a column store that buffers writes in row-wise delta structures
A column store with a larger page size
Either; layout does not affect update cost
explain: Each update touches every column, so a pure column layout would write into one place per column. Row stores write one contiguous record. Column stores cope by sending writes to delta structures (as MonetDB/X100 does) and merging later.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
question: Why does the branch-free select loop write res[k] = i even for rows that fail the predicate?
options: It is a bug that wastes memory
Because the selection vector must have length n
So the loop has no data-dependent branch; a failing row's write is simply overwritten by the next one
To keep the output sorted
explain: Writing unconditionally and advancing k by the 0/1 comparison result removes the branch. With unpredictable predicates this avoids branch mispredictions; the stray write is harmless since k did not advance.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops
question: A loop over `float *out, const float *in` with a runtime length n is not vectorized at `gcc -O2` but is at -O3. What is the most likely reason?
options: -O2 does not support SIMD instructions
-O2's very-cheap cost model rejects loops that need a runtime alias check
Floats can never be vectorized at -O2
The loop needs -march=native first
explain: With runtime n and two pointers that may overlap, vectorizing needs a runtime overlap check. The very-cheap model used at -O2 refuses any runtime alias check (and, before GCC 15, any loop needing a scalar epilogue); -O3's dynamic model accepts them. restrict (plus a known trip count on GCC 14 and older) can make -O2 vectorize it.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
question: You build a CLI tool on a new workstation with `-O2 -march=native` and publish the binary for all Linux x86-64 users. What is the main risk?
options: It runs slower on older CPUs
It produces different numeric results on AMD
It may use instructions older CPUs lack, so it fails to run there
Nothing, -march only affects scheduling
explain: -march=native enables every extension of the build machine, and GCC's manual warns the result might not run elsewhere. For a distributed binary use the default target, a psABI level like x86-64-v2 or v3 that you document, or runtime dispatch (ship several versions of the hot code and pick one at startup from the CPU's features). -mtune changes scheduling only.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Coordinates: grounding a click and scaling it to the real display
question: Clicks land in the right area but often miss very small targets. Scaling is verified correct. Which fix matches the docs' guidance?
options: Send the screenshot at a higher resolution than the image limit so the API keeps detail
Switch the aspect ratio of the screenshot to 1:1 so the model counts pixels more easily
Keep zoom enabled so the model can inspect the region at full resolution, and keep the aspect ratio when resizing
Retry each click three times at random offsets of a few pixels
explain: The docs attribute right-area misses to tiny targets, detail lost when downscaling a large source, or distorted aspect ratio, and suggest zoom, cropping or capturing at lower DPI (dots per inch), and preserving aspect ratio. Oversized images are rejected, not kept. Random retries can click the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
question: Your lock-free queue test passed 50,000 times on an x86 laptop. A teammate says it is now safe to ship to Arm servers. What is the strongest objection?
options: 50,000 runs is too few; 5 million runs would be enough
x86 hardware keeps more orderings than Arm, so a missing Release or Acquire may simply be invisible there and still break on Arm
The test should have been run in debug mode instead of release mode
Lock-free code cannot be tested at all, only proven
explain: Running more often only samples more schedules of the same hardware memory model. Weak-ordering bugs that x86's stronger hardware ordering hides have probability zero there, so no count of x86 runs covers them. A tool that models the language memory model, like loom, can explore those executions.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
question: A CI job runs your C++ service's integration tests under `-fsanitize=thread` and reports nothing for months. Which statement is justified?
options: The service is free of data races
TSan is misconfigured, since every large program has races
The service cannot deadlock
No data race occurred, unordered by happens-before, on the code paths and synchronization these tests exercised
explain: TSan is a dynamic detector: it is precise about what it saw but blind to paths that never ran and to races hidden by incidental synchronization in this run. Clean reports are evidence about the executed paths only.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
question: You need a one-step text-to-image model and have no budget for training a new diffusion model, but you do have a strong pretrained latent diffusion model with classifier-free guidance. Which approach fits best?
